claims.text: Friction stir processing with in-situ TiC nanoparticle injection will create a refined, ultrafine-grained surface layer in nickel-based superalloys or high-strength steels.
The processed surface layer will contain uniformly dispersed TiC nanoparticles integrated into a composite structure.
Friction stir processing induces dynamic recrystallization that refines the surface grain structure.
Mechanical stirring during friction stir processing uniformly disperses the injected TiC nanoparticles.
The refined TiC-reinforced structure increases surface hardness.
The intervention introduces beneficial residual compressive stresses.
The combined grain refinement, TiC reinforcement, and residual stresses inhibit crack nucleation and propagation.
The treated surface will have at least 20% greater hardness than both fusion-welded repair surfaces and untreated surfaces.
The treated surface will have better wear resistance than both fusion-welded repair surfaces and untreated surfaces.
The treated surface will have better corrosion resistance than both fusion-welded repair surfaces and untreated surfaces.
The friction-stir-processed repair will avoid hot cracking.
The intervention will delay surface-defect initiation in aggressive environments.
The intervention is expected to be effective when processing remains below the alloy melting temperature.
Extremely severe damage or deviation from the processing parameters could reduce the effectiveness of the repair.
The magnitude of improvement depends on processing-parameter optimization and TiC dispersion quality.

contradictions.description: The FSP condition requires a below-melting, solid-state temperature, but the experiment states that fusion-welded controls and FSP specimens are processed under identical temperature conditions; conventional fusion welding necessarily requires local melting.
